questions.q: Per this lesson, what skill do Salesforce architect-track scenario questions actually test?
options: Memorizing every Salesforce feature name in alphabetical order
Extracting the few facts that actually answer the four framing questions from the surrounding detail, then reasoning to the option that fits those facts
Recognizing which answer option uses the most technical-sounding vocabulary
Calculating exact governor limit numbers from memory
questions.explain: The tested skill, per this lesson, is the same one from Lesson 11: pulling out the facts that answer who initiates, how often, how much data, and how fast, and reasoning from there — not memorizing facts or picking the most sophisticated-sounding wording.

questions.q: In Scenario 1 (the Order-confirmation email with an explicitly non-blocking requirement and an acceptable few-minute delay), what does this lesson say those details rule out immediately?
options: They rule out using Bulk API
They rule out any synchronous option, since the scenario explicitly says no part of the process should be blocked and a short delay is fine
They rule out using a Platform Event
They rule out using Salesforce as the initiator
questions.explain: The explicit 'no blocking allowed' and 'a few minutes is fine' details directly rule out synchronous communication, pointing instead to a fire-and-forget pattern such as a Platform Event.

questions.q: In Scenario 3 (real-time inventory check with documented 99.9% uptime and 300ms typical response time), what does this lesson say is actually the deciding factor for choosing synchronous communication?
options: The 99.9% uptime figure alone, regardless of anything else in the scenario
The urgency answer — the rep is blocked and cannot proceed without the answer right now — with the uptime and latency figures serving as reassuring context rather than the deciding factor
The fact that inventory data changes frequently
The specific vendor that built the warehouse system
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly notes that the uptime and latency statistics are reassuring context, not the deciding factor — the real deciding factor remains the urgency answer: the business process genuinely cannot proceed without an immediate response.

questions.q: In Scenario 4 (three systems notified on Contract activation, with an explicit requirement that adding a fourth system next year shouldn't require changing the activation logic), which pattern does this requirement point to almost by name?
options: Point-to-point integration
Synchronous RPC-style invocation
Event-driven architecture, because of its explicit decoupling benefit that lets new consumers be added without touching the producer
A full data migration pattern
questions.explain: The explicit requirement that a new consumer shouldn't require changing the producer's logic is exactly EDA's decoupling benefit from Lesson 8 — any point-to-point-style answer requiring the producer to change for a new consumer would be wrong by definition here.

questions.q: What frequent exam-writing pattern does this lesson warn test-takers to watch for?
options: Every answer option is always equally correct, so guessing is as good as reasoning

An option that is technically correct in isolation but ignores a specific stated constraint (like volume or a non-blocking requirement), presented alongside the genuinely correct option that respects every fact given
Exam questions never include any irrelevant detail
The correct answer is always the shortest option listed
questions.explain: A common distractor is technically sound on its own but silently ignores a constraint the scenario explicitly stated — the discipline this lesson teaches is treating every given fact as load-bearing rather than skimming for a familiar keyword.
